item.text: {"answers":[{"question_id":"Q009_heme_bundle_fold_not_homology","answer":"No. SCOPe 2.08 places these proteins in three separate superfamilies within fold f.21, “Heme-binding four-helical bundle” (SUNID 81344): transmembrane di-heme cytochromes, f.21.1 (81342); fumarate reductase respiratory complex transmembrane subunits, f.21.2 (81343); and respiratory nitrate reductase 1 gamma chain, f.21.3 (103501). Their shared class is f, “Membrane and cell surface proteins and peptides.” The fold comprises four transmembrane helices in an up-and-down bundle, binding one or two hemes between the helices.\n\nThese are distinct superfamilies, not merely different families within one homologous superfamily. Families group closer evolutionary relatives; superfamilies support probable common ancestry, whereas shared fold or class alone does not imply homology. Separate superfamilies do not prove independent origins, but SCOPe does not establish common ancestry across these three groups. Shared architecture and heme binding therefore cannot justify transferring specific respiratory function, substrate specificity, or mechanistic details. A cross-superfamily structure can suggest a broad architectural template, but reliable detailed modeling requires validated alignment and topology; one representative cannot stand for all three evolutionary groups. Establishing a broader homologous relationship would require independent sequence/profile and detailed structural evolutionary evidence, and specific functional transfer would require biochemical support.","evidence_used":["/api/v1/","/api/v1/openapi.yaml","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=heme-binding","/api/v1/releases/2.08/search?q=di-heme","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/81344","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/81344/children","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/81344/homology","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/56835","/api/v1/releases/2.08/sunids/81344/annotations"]}]}
